board.name: Board X
board.note: Fictional product used by every case in this course. The numbers are consistent across modules; nothing here describes a real customer board.
board.description: 6-layer 1.6 mm FR-4 controller board: QFP-64 at 0.5 mm pitch, QFP-48 at 0.4 mm pitch, one 256-ball BGA at 0.8 mm, 0402 passives, and one 20-pin THT connector.

facts.thtConnector: 20-pin, 2.54 mm pitch, 0.8 mm finished hole, 0.5 mm lead

cases.title: Stencil release audit: the QFP-48 apertures will not release
scenario: Board X goes to a new stencil supplier. The first article prints clean on the 0402 passives and on the 0.5 mm QFP-64, but the 0.4 mm QFP-48 pads come up short in SPI: low volume on the inner rows, no offset, no bridging.

The stencil drawing issued to the supplier carries a single foil thickness of 0.125 mm and apertures of 0.20 mm x 0.80 mm on the fine-pitch part. Before you blame the printer, check whether the aperture geometry can release paste at all, and what the cheapest geometry change is that fixes it without touching the 0.5 mm part or the passives.
Work through the release indicators in the order the course uses them: area ratio, aspect ratio, then the aperture change. Use the aperture table in the data file.

dataFiles.name: aperture-table.csv
dataFiles.content:
aperture_id,component,shape,width_mm,length_mm,diameter_mm,foil_mm,pitch_mm
A-01,0402 passive,rect,0.55,0.60,,0.125,0.50
A-02,QFP-64 0.5 mm,rect,0.22,0.90,,0.125,0.50
A-03,QFP-48 0.4 mm (current),rect,0.20,0.80,,0.125,0.40
A-04,QFP-48 0.4 mm (thin region),rect,0.20,0.80,,0.100,0.40
A-05,BGA 0.8 mm,round,,,0.50,0.125,0.80
A-06,THT connector,rect,0.18,0.80,,0.125,2.54

steps.prompt: Aperture A-03 (QFP-48, 0.20 mm x 0.80 mm, 0.125 mm foil). Area ratio = (L x W) / (2 x (L + W) x T). Give the value to two decimals.
hints: The wall area is the perimeter times the foil thickness, and the perimeter of a rectangle is 2 x (L + W).
Numerator 0.20 x 0.80 = 0.160 mm². Denominator 2 x (0.20 + 0.80) x 0.125 = 0.250 mm².
0.160 / 0.250 = 0.64. Below the 0.66 release indicator the course uses.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 0.64 — below the 0.66 release indicator, so the aperture is the first suspect.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the order of operations: area on top, perimeter times thickness underneath.
steps.explanation: Area ratio is (L x W) / (2 x (L + W) x T). For 0.20 x 0.80 at T = 0.125 the numerator is 0.160 mm² and the denominator 0.250 mm², giving 0.64. That is below the 0.66 guidance the course takes from IPC-7525, which is why release fails before any printer setting is touched.

steps.prompt: Against the release indicator the course uses, what does 0.64 mean for A-03?

options.text: Acceptable: it is above 0.60, the practical floor for a laser-cut foil.
Marginal to inadequate: it is below the 0.66 guidance, so release depends on paste rheology and SPI evidence, not on geometry alone.
Acceptable, because area ratio only matters below 0.5.
Irrelevant, because aspect ratio is the only release indicator.

hints: The lesson treats 0.66 as guidance rather than a wall, and asks what supports a marginal aperture.
0.64 is 0.02 under the indicator — close enough that some pastes will run it, which is exactly why it is called marginal.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Marginal — 0.64 sits just under the 0.66 guidance, so release is not guaranteed by geometry.
steps.feedbackWrong: Re-read the lesson's wording: it gives a guidance value and then says what evidence can support an aperture below it.
steps.explanation: The course calls apertures below 0.66 marginal to inadequate: they may run with a favourable paste and a well-cut wall, but the release is then supported by SPI data and paste evidence rather than by geometry. 0.60 is not a floor the course states, and area ratio is not the only indicator — aspect ratio is its partner.

steps.prompt: Same aperture printed through the 0.100 mm stepped region (A-04). What is the area ratio now?
hints: The perimeter does not change when the foil gets thinner; only the denominator's second factor changes.
Denominator becomes 2 x (0.20 + 0.80) x 0.100 = 0.200 mm².
steps.feedbackCorrect: 0.80 — comfortably clear of the 0.66 indicator.
steps.feedbackWrong: Only the foil thickness changed: keep the numerator at 0.160 mm² and redo the denominator.
steps.explanation: At 0.100 mm the wall area drops to 0.200 mm², so the ratio rises to 0.80. That is the step-stencil remedy: thin the foil only over the fine-pitch region, because the reduction in wall contact is what buys the release.

steps.prompt: For that same 0.20 mm aperture in 0.100 mm foil, what is the aspect ratio?
hints: Aspect ratio uses the smallest aperture dimension, not the length.
Aspect ratio = aperture width / foil thickness.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 2.0 — above the 1.5 indicator as well.
steps.feedbackWrong: Use the narrow dimension (0.20 mm), divided by the foil thickness.
steps.explanation: Aspect ratio = smallest dimension / foil thickness = 0.20 / 0.100 = 2.0, above the 1.5 guidance. Both indicators now pass, so the geometry argument for the step stencil is complete.

steps.prompt: The THT connector aperture A-06 is 0.18 mm x 0.80 mm in 0.125 mm foil. What is its area ratio?
hints: Same formula as before; the narrow dimension drives the result.
Numerator 0.18 x 0.80 = 0.144 mm², denominator 2 x (0.18 + 0.80) x 0.125 = 0.245 mm².
steps.feedbackCorrect: 0.59 — the worst aperture on the board.
steps.feedbackWrong: Recompute both the area and the perimeter for the narrower aperture.
steps.explanation: 0.144 / 0.245 = 0.588, so 0.59. It is the lowest ratio on Board X and would be the second candidate for a step-down region if the connector pads show short deposits.

steps.prompt: The BGA aperture A-05 is a round 0.50 mm opening in 0.125 mm foil. For a circle the area ratio is D / (4 x T). What is it?
hints: For a circle the perimeter is pi x D and the area is pi x D² / 4, so pi cancels.
What is left is D / (4 x T).
steps.feedbackCorrect: 1.00 — a comfortable margin, as the round aperture should give.
steps.feedbackWrong: Use D / (4 x T) directly; do not square the diameter.
steps.explanation: Area ratio for a round aperture is D / (4 x T) = 0.50 / 0.500 = 1.00. The pi terms cancel between the circular area and the circular wall, which is why round BGA openings tolerate a thicker foil than a narrow rectangle at the same dimension.

steps.prompt: How much paste does the 0.20 x 0.80 mm aperture hold in 0.100 mm foil, in nanolithres? (1 mm³ = 1000 nL)
hints: Nominal volume is aperture area times foil thickness.
0.016 mm³ x 1000 nL/mm³ = 16 nL.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 16 nL of nominal volume per aperture.
steps.feedbackWrong: Watch the unit: the volume in mm³ is smaller than the number in nL by a factor of 1000.
steps.explanation: Aperture area 0.160 mm² times foil 0.100 mm gives 0.016 mm³, which is 16 nL. Compare that with the joint requirement before choosing foil: thinner foil fixes release but reduces volume, which is why the two checks are a loop.

steps.prompt: Which change fixes A-03 without disturbing the 0.5 mm QFP-64 and the passives?

options.text: Reduce the whole stencil to 0.100 mm.
Step the foil down to 0.100 mm over the QFP-48 region only.
Raise squeegee pressure until the apertures fill.
Reduce the aperture width to 0.18 mm to lower the wall contact.

hints: Which parts of the board are already printing inside the indicators?
A-01 and A-02 sit comfortably above 0.66 at 0.125 mm, so a global change would move them for no reason.
The course's step-stencil lesson: put the transition away from fine-pitch features and keep each region at its own thickness.
steps.feedbackCorrect: A stepped region at 0.100 mm over the fine-pitch part only.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the ratios of the other apertures at 0.125 mm before choosing a global change.
steps.explanation: A-01 (0402) and A-02 (QFP-64 at 0.22 x 0.90) already pass at 0.125 mm, so thinning the whole foil would cut their paste volume for nothing and can cause its own defects. A stepped foil gives the QFP-48 the 0.80 it needs while leaving the rest of the board where it printed well. Pressure cannot repair a wall-dominated release, and a narrower aperture lowers the ratio further.

rubric.criterion: Area ratio of the current fine-pitch aperture computed correctly
Result judged against the release indicator, not against intuition
Thinned-foil area ratio recomputed from geometry
Aspect ratio computed with the narrow dimension
Second-worst aperture identified and quantified
Round-aperture rule applied, not the rectangle formula
Nominal volume converted to nanolithres without a factor error
Remedy chosen that does not move the apertures already in spec

cases.title: Moisture breach: the BGA reel sat in a 7 % RH cabinet
scenario: Board X's 256-ball BGA comes in on MSL 4 tape and reel. The reel was opened 58 h ago and went straight into the storage dry cabinet. The cabinet log shows 7 % RH for the whole period; the setpoint in the procedure is 5 %.
During the second shift a feeder was loaded and the reel sat on the machine for 6 h before the line went down. Reflow of that build is planned 10 h from now.
Decide the disposition. The lesson is explicit that a cabinet above the dry-storage requirement does not stop the clock, and that a tape-and-reel bake has a hard temperature ceiling.

steps.prompt: What is the J-STD-033 floor life for MSL 4, in hours at the reference condition?
hints: The values in the course run 168 h, 72 h, 48 h, 24 h down the levels.
MSL 4 is the third value in that sequence.
MSL 4 = 72 h.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 72 h — the number the whole disposition hangs on.
steps.feedbackWrong: This is a table lookup, not an arithmetic result: MSL 4 is 72 h.
steps.explanation: MSL 4 has 72 h of floor life at 30 °C / 60 % RH. MSL 3 is 168 h and MSL 5 is 48 h, which is why the levels are always quoted with their value.

steps.prompt: How many hours count against that floor life? Add the bag-open period and the time on the open feeder.
hints: A 7 % RH cabinet is above the 5 % requirement, so the cabinet time is not suspended.
The 6 h on the feeder is outside the cabinet entirely.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 64 h counted — the cabinet gave no credit at 7 % RH.
steps.feedbackWrong: Every hour counts here: the cabinet was not compliant, so nothing is discounted.
steps.explanation: A cabinet at 7 % RH is above the 5 % dry-storage requirement, so exposure keeps accumulating; the 6 h on the open feeder adds on top. 58 + 6 = 64 h of a 72 h budget.

steps.prompt: How much floor life is left for the BGA reel, in hours?
hints: Subtract the counted exposure from the floor life.
72 h minus 64 h.
8 h remain, against a reflow planned in 10 h.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 8 h left, and the reflow is 10 h away — the reel cannot simply proceed.
steps.feedbackWrong: Floor life minus counted exposure, in hours.
steps.explanation: 72 - 64 = 8 h remain, but the planned reflow is 10 h away. The batch is 2 h short, so the decision is bake or reschedule, not release.

steps.prompt: The cabinet logged 7 % RH against a 5 % requirement. What does the course say that does to the clock?

options.text: It suspends the clock, because any dry cabinet below 10 % RH is equivalent to sealed dry pack.
It slows the clock, but 5 % RH or less is the condition that suspends it, so this storage gave no credit.
It resets the clock, because the parts were dry when they went in.
It has no effect either way; only the bag seal matters.

hints: The lesson was corrected on exactly this point: 10 % RH is not the requirement.
5 % RH or less is what stops moisture uptake; above it the budget keeps shrinking, just more slowly.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Correct — 7 % RH slows the clock but does not suspend it, so no credit was given.
steps.feedbackWrong: Look at which relative humidity the lesson calls the requirement, not which is common on a cheap cabinet.
steps.explanation: Below 5 % RH the device stops gaining moisture, so the exposure clock is suspended. A 10 % cabinet is common and slows the clock rather than stopping it; at 7 % the parts were outside the requirement, so the full 64 h counts. The 10 % form is a mitigation for devices with budget to spare, never a substitute for the requirement.

steps.prompt: The reel needs a bake. What is the maximum temperature the tape and reel may see, in °C?
hints: Carrier tape and cover tape soften and deform when they get hot.
The lesson gives a fixed ceiling for tape and reel, not a range.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 40 °C — and at 40 °C the bake takes days, not hours.
steps.feedbackWrong: The value is a fixed ceiling in the lesson, well below the 125 °C tray bake.
steps.explanation: Tape and reel must not be baked above 40 °C because the carrier and cover tape deform. At that temperature the table runs to days for a thin body, which is why the 40 °C route does not fit a 10 h window.

steps.prompt: The reflow is 10 h away and a 40 °C bake will not finish in time. Which route does the lesson support?

options.text: Bake the reel at 125 °C for 7 h and accept some tape deformation.
De-reel into trays, bake the loose parts at the permitted higher temperature, then re-reel; or move the build inside the remaining floor life.
Skip the bake and raise the reflow peak by 10 °C to drive the moisture out.
Run the reel as-is and inspect the BGA after reflow.

hints: Which constraint is physical and which is scheduling?
The tape ceiling is a material limit; the schedule is not. The lesson offers de-reeling and rescheduling.
De-reel to a carrier that tolerates 125 °C, or move the reflow inside the 8 h.
steps.feedbackCorrect: De-reel and bake at the higher temperature, or move the build inside the remaining floor life.
steps.feedbackWrong: The lesson never trades a material limit for a schedule.
steps.explanation: Baking a reel at 125 °C destroys the carrier tape, and raising the peak adds thermal stress without removing moisture. The two supported routes are de-reeling to a carrier rated for the 125 °C bake, or rescheduling the build inside the 8 h that remain. Reflowing an unbaked MSL 4 batch and inspecting afterwards turns a known risk into a detection gamble.

rubric.criterion: Floor life for MSL 4 taken from the table, not guessed
Exposure counted with no credit for a non-compliant cabinet
Remaining life computed and compared with the reflow schedule
7 % RH judged against the 5 % requirement
Tape-and-reel bake ceiling known
Route chosen that respects the material limit

cases.title: Profile validation: Board X runs a 248 °C peak
scenario: Board X is a 1.6 mm six-layer board with heavy ground planes and a large BGA. The thermal survey from the worst-case site gives the profile in the data file: 25 to 150 °C in 60 s, soak 150 to 190 °C for 90 s, 65 s above 219 °C, peak 248 °C, and cooling from 248 to 100 °C in 40 s.
Paste is SAC305 with a datasheet window of 60-90 s above liquidus and a peak of 245-250 °C. The BGA is a large package, so the J-STD-020 classification temperature that applies to it is 250 °C.
Validate the profile, compute the margins, and decide whether it can be released with a documentation note or must be changed.

dataFiles.name: profile.csv
dataFiles.content:
interval,from_c,to_c,seconds,rate_c_per_s
ramp,25,150,60,
soak,150,190,90,
approach,190,219,30,
above_liquidus,219,248,65,
peak_hold,248,248,4,
cooling,248,100,40,

steps.prompt: What is the ramp rate from 25 °C to 150 °C, in °C/s?
hints: Rate is a temperature difference over a time.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 2.08 °C/s — inside the 1-3 °C/s guidance.
steps.feedbackWrong: Divide the rise by the seconds, not the other way round.
steps.explanation: 125 °C in 60 s gives 2.08 °C/s, which sits inside the 1-3 °C/s guidance the course takes from IPC-7530. This is the figure the m06 lesson works, and it matters because a ramp that is too fast drives tombstoning on the 0402s.

steps.prompt: The profile gives 65 s above 219 °C. Against the paste datasheet window of 60-90 s, how many seconds of margin are there at the lower end?
hints: The window opens at 60 s.
65 s minus 60 s.
5 s of margin.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 5 s above the lower bound — inside the window, with little margin.
steps.feedbackWrong: Subtract the window minimum from the measured time above liquidus.
steps.explanation: 65 s clears the 60 s floor of the paste window by 5 s. The course treats that as passing but thin: a slower line or a colder zone could drop the board below the window without anyone changing the recipe.

steps.prompt: Peak is 248 °C and the large-package classification temperature is 250 °C. What margin is left, in °C?
hints: Margin is limit minus measured, not measured minus limit.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 2 °C of margin to the classification limit.
steps.feedbackWrong: The limit is the upper number; subtract the measurement from it.
steps.explanation: 250 - 248 leaves 2 °C. The classification temperature is a ceiling for the package, so a 2 °C margin means any zone drift or heavier board can push the peak over it — worth a note in the profile record even though the profile passes.

steps.prompt: Cooling runs from 248 °C to 100 °C in 40 s. What is the cooling rate in °C/s?
hints: Same rate formula, with the drop as the temperature difference.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 3.7 °C/s — fast cooling, good for grain structure but hard on large components.
steps.feedbackWrong: Use the drop (148 °C) over the 40 s cooling window.
steps.explanation: 148 °C in 40 s is 3.7 °C/s. The course notes that cooling that fast is good for fine grain but raises the thermal gradient across a large BGA, so it is a parameter to record and watch rather than a defect.

steps.prompt: Which disposition does the profile earn?

options.text: Reject and change the profile: the peak is over the 245 °C limit.
Accept and document: peak and time above liquidus are inside their windows, with 2 °C and 5 s of margin noted in the profile record.
Reject: time above liquidus must always exceed 90 s on a heavy board.
Accept without comment: a profile only fails if the joints look wrong.

hints: Which limit applies to a large package — 245 °C or 250 °C?
The 245 °C figure belongs to the very large package class; the course lists 250 °C for a large one.
Peak and TAL both pass with thin margins, so the record carries the margins.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Accept and document, with both thin margins written into the profile record.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check which package class Board X's BGA falls in before comparing against 245 °C.
steps.explanation: For a large package the classification temperature is 250 °C, so 248 °C passes with 2 °C to spare; the 245 °C limit belongs to the very large class the course describes separately. Time above liquidus 65 s is inside the 60-90 s paste window. The honest disposition is accept-and-document, because the margins are thin enough that the record has to carry them.

steps.prompt: A first-principles check: the oven delivers about 100 W and the board's measured thermal mass is 90 J/K. What ramp rate does that predict, in °C/s?
hints: Ramp rate from heat input is power divided by thermal mass.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 1.1 °C/s predicted, against 2.08 °C/s measured.
steps.feedbackWrong: Power over thermal mass; the units work out to °C/s directly.
steps.explanation: 100 / 90 = 1.1 °C/s, roughly half the measured ramp. The model is a sanity check, not an oracle: the real oven adds zone power and the board receives radiated heat, so a measured rate above the model is expected — but a factor of two is worth checking before the model is used to set a recipe.

steps.prompt: What should be done with the factor-of-two gap between the model and the measurement?

options.text: Trust the model: the measured thermocouple must be wrong.
Trust the measurement and record the model's assumptions as unvalidated for this board; re-measure a second worst-case site before using the model to predict zone settings.
Average the two values and use that as the ramp rate.
Ignore both and use the paste datasheet ramp figure.

hints: A thermocouple on the worst-case site is direct evidence; a lumped model is an estimate.
The lesson's own wording is to treat the model as an estimate and verify against measurement.
Keep the measurement, flag the model, and take a second site.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Keep the measurement, mark the model unvalidated for Board X, and check a second worst-case site.
steps.feedbackWrong: The question is which number is evidence and which is an assumption.
steps.explanation: The thermocouple is direct evidence; the 100 W / 90 J/K model is a lumped estimate that ignores radiation, zone coupling and board mass distribution. Averaging an estimate with a measurement produces a number with no physical meaning, and the datasheet ramp is a paste guideline, not this board's behaviour. Record the gap and re-measure a second site before the model is trusted.

rubric.criterion: Ramp rate computed from the recorded interval
Time above liquidus compared with the paste window
Peak margin taken against the correct package class
Cooling rate computed and interpreted
Disposition states the margins rather than just 'pass'
Model-versus-measurement check performed
Evidence ranked above the estimate

cases.title: AOI over-rejection on Board X: DPMO, sampling scope and an 8D that is not closed
scenario: Board X runs 1,240 boards a day with 620 solder opportunities per board. Last week AOI raised 47 calls against the BGA and the fine-pitch QFP; the defect review confirmed 38 of them and threw 9 out as false calls.

The 8D team contained the suspect lot and needs a sampling plan for the retroactive search: one lot is 3,000 boards, another is 5,000. The control plan requires ISO 2859-1 general inspection level II at AQL 1.0.
A corrective action has been running for six weeks on a different defect family: 96 defects in 6,000 boards before, 21 defects in 7,500 boards after. The agreed effectiveness target is 1,000 ppm.
Compute the metrics the 8D needs, and be honest about what the numbers do and do not prove.

steps.prompt: Compute DPMO for Board X from the confirmed defects. DPMO = defects / (boards x opportunities per board) x 1,000,000. One decimal.
hints: Use confirmed defects, not AOI calls.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 49.4 DPMO — computed from confirmed defects only.
steps.feedbackWrong: Multiply boards by opportunities first, then divide, then scale to a million.
steps.explanation: 38 / (1,240 x 620) = 38 / 768,800 = 4.94 x 10^-5, which is 49.4 defects per million opportunities. Using the 47 AOI calls instead would inflate the number to about 61 DPMO and turn an inspection problem into a process problem.

steps.prompt: AOI raised 47 calls of which 38 were confirmed. What is the false-call rate, in percent? One decimal.
hints: The false calls are the calls that did not survive review.
47 - 38 = 9 false calls out of 47 calls.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 19.1 % false calls — an inspection capability issue, not a solder issue.
steps.feedbackWrong: Divide the false calls by the total calls, not by the confirmed defects.
steps.explanation: 9 / 47 = 19.1 %. The course treats false calls as a separate metric from escape rate: a high false-call rate costs review time and erodes trust in the station, but it does not put a bad board in the field the way an escape does.

steps.prompt: For a lot of 3,000 boards, what is the ISO 2859-1 code letter at general inspection level II?

options.text: J
K
L
M

hints: The lot-size ranges for level II step at 1,200 and at 3,200.
3,000 falls in the 1,201-3,200 band.
That band is code K: n = 125 at AQL 1.0.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Code K for 3,000 boards: sample 125, Ac 3, Re 4.
steps.feedbackWrong: Find the lot-size band first; the letter follows from the band, not from the count.
steps.explanation: At general inspection level II a lot of 3,000 sits in the 1,201-3,200 band, which is code K: 125 pieces sampled, accept at 3, reject at 4 for AQL 1.0. Code L belongs to the next band (3,201-10,000) and code J to the one below (501-1,200).

steps.prompt: For that 3,000-board lot at code K, AQL 1.0, how many pieces are sampled?
hints: Code K fixes the sample size.
It is the n column for K, not a percentage of the lot.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 125 pieces sampled.
steps.feedbackWrong: This is a table lookup for code K at AQL 1.0.
steps.explanation: Code K samples 125 pieces. The accept number is 3 and the reject number 4, so finding 3 or fewer nonconforming units accepts the lot and 4 rejects it — the plan is not a zero-defect rule.

steps.prompt: The retroactive search on the 3,000-board lot finds 3 nonconforming boards. What does the plan say?

options.text: Reject the lot: any nonconformity in a containment sample fails it.
Accept the lot against this plan (Ac = 3), while the 8D still has to explain the three units found.
Accept the lot and close the 8D.
Reject and double the sample until zero defects are found.

hints: Ac is the acceptance number for the plan, and it is not zero.
Ac = 3 means 3 or fewer accepts; Re = 4 is the reject threshold.
Accepting the lot on the sampling plan does not close the 8D.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Accept against Ac = 3, and keep the 8D open — sampling says nothing about the cause.
steps.feedbackWrong: Separate the sampling decision from the corrective-action decision.
steps.explanation: At AQL 1.0 code K the acceptance number is 3, so three nonconforming boards accept the lot. That is a statement about the lot against an agreed quality level, not evidence that the cause is fixed: acceptance sampling with Ac > 0 always passes some nonconforming units, which is why the 8D is closed on the effectiveness metric, not on the sample.

steps.prompt: The second lot is 5,000 boards at the same level and AQL. How many pieces does the plan sample?
hints: 5,000 falls in the 3,201-10,000 band.
That band is code L.
Code L samples 200 pieces: Ac 5, Re 6.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 200 pieces at code L (Ac 5, Re 6).
steps.feedbackWrong: Find the band for 5,000 first, then read n for that code.
steps.explanation: 5,000 boards is code L, which samples 200 pieces with Ac 5 and Re 6 at AQL 1.0. Note that the sample grows far more slowly than the lot: doubling the lot from 3,000 to 5,000 raises the sample from 125 to 200, which is why sampling alone cannot bound a large escape.

steps.prompt: Corrective-action window: 96 defects in 6,000 boards. What is that rate in ppm?
hints: ppm is defects per million boards.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 16,000 ppm before the action.
steps.feedbackWrong: Divide defects by boards, then multiply by a million.
steps.explanation: 96 / 6,000 = 0.016, which is 16,000 defects per million boards. Stating it in ppm rather than percent keeps the comparison with the 1,000 ppm target in one scale.

steps.prompt: After the action: 21 defects in 7,500 boards. What is the rate in ppm?
hints: Same conversion as the before figure.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 2,800 ppm after the action.
steps.feedbackWrong: Defects over boards, then scale to a million.
steps.explanation: 21 / 7,500 = 0.0028, so 2,800 ppm. The two windows are different lengths, which is exactly why the comparison is made on a rate and not on a defect count.

steps.prompt: What is the reduction between the two rates, in percent? One decimal.
hints: Reduction is measured against the before rate.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 82.5 % reduction — a real improvement, and still not the target.
steps.feedbackWrong: Divide the improvement by the before rate, then multiply by 100.
steps.explanation: (16,000 - 2,800) / 16,000 = 82.5 %. An 82.5 % reduction sounds like success until it is put against the target: 2,800 ppm is still nearly three times the agreed 1,000 ppm, so by the metric the course uses the action is not yet effective.

steps.prompt: The effectiveness target is 1,000 ppm and the after rate is 2,800 ppm. What is the correct 8D status?

options.text: Close the 8D: an 82.5 % reduction is a passing result.
Keep the 8D open: the action improved the rate but did not reach the agreed metric, so effectiveness is not demonstrated.
Close the 8D and open a new one for the residual 2,800 ppm.
Change the target to 3,000 ppm so the action passes.

hints: Effectiveness is judged against the metric agreed before the action.
The course closes an 8D on the metric, not on the improvement.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Keep it open — the improvement is real, the target is not met.
steps.feedbackWrong: Which number was agreed before the action started?
steps.explanation: An 82.5 % improvement with a residual rate nearly three times the target is a partial result. The course's rule is that the 8D stays open until the effectiveness metric is met with evidence; renegotiating the target after the fact destroys the point of having one, and opening a second 8D for the same cause just moves the paperwork.

rubric.criterion: DPMO computed from confirmed defects with the right denominator
False-call rate computed separately from defect rate
Correct ISO 2859-1 code letter for the lot size
Sample size read for the code, not guessed
Accept/reject decision separated from cause and closure
Second lot handled with its own code and sample
Before and after rates expressed in the same unit
After rate computed on its own window
Reduction computed against the before rate
8D status judged on the agreed metric, not on the improvement
